new_statements.rule_in_words: Borna/Shinasha is a tone language (H vs L, with a debated third/extra-high level); there is no phonological word stress. Corroborated first-hand by Ashenafi Tesfaye & Wedekind 1990: 351 (saved file): 'Stress is used occasionally to express emphasis. Apart from this pragmatic function, stress is not phonetically noticeable.' and 352: unlike Cushitic neighbours, word shape and morpheme class do not determine stress and pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress used occasionally for emphasis (pragmatic only) per Ashenafi & Wedekind 1990: 351; Rottland 1990: 189 (as quoted) allowed that vowel elision/epenthesis tied to L/H tone might be stress-linked; Lamberti 1993 marks stress and calls the final unvoiced vowel 'meistens unbetont' (mostly unstressed), which Bergfjord rejects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology (Bergfjord's thesis is explicitly word-level; citation forms are the predicative -a form). Tone: Ashenafi & Wedekind and Bikila 2018 give two levels H/L; Bergfjord argues a three-level analysis is needed for some forms; Rottland and Lamberti posit three levels.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language under the names Borna (autonym), Shinasha/Shinassha/Šinaša (exonym) and Boro/Bworo = boro1277 [bwo]. Bergfjord's data come from speakers from Dibati wäräda (Benishangul-Gumuz); Ashenafi & Wedekind's from Metekel; Bikila and Tsehay from the Bulen/Debati varieties. Two mutually intelligible dialects (lowland/highland; Worwi-Bora vs Gayi-Bora) are mentioned; no separate glottocodes.
